newsitem.title: FRANCE: French minister rejects Corsican separatist demands.
newsitem.headline: French minister rejects Corsican separatist demands.

text.p: French Interior Minister Jean-Louis Chevenement, ending his first visit to Corsica, on Friday rejected separatist demands and urged a halt to bombings to help to revive the island's economy.

"France is a nation of citizens and not founded on ethnic groups," he said, ruling out nationalist calls for autonomy including official recognition of a "Corsican people" and a "Corsican language" on the Mediterranean island.

Chevenement, who travelled under tight guard to the main towns of Ajaccio and Bastia, said France's six-week-old Socialist-led government believed the "firm and calm application" of the law was a condition for the island's development.
"Nothing is possible without security, without the end of violence, without the definitive return of civic peace," he said repeatedly during the two-day visit.

Thousands of separatist bombs have exploded on Corsica, an island of 250,000 people where tourism is a main money earner, over the past two decades. Most were aimed at buildings symbolising state authority like post offices or law courts.
Criminal gangs also set off bombs as part of extortion rackets. Casualties have been few.
A bomb exploded on Thursday night at a racetrack at Viseo in southern Corsica, destroying two stands but causing no casualties. No one claimed responsibility.
Corsican militants reacted tepidly to Chevenement's visit.

Jean-Guy Talamoni, member of the A Cuncolta Naziunalista group, the political front of the outlawed FLNC-Historical Wing, said militants were ready for talks but also "prepared to resume the struggle."
The FLNC declared a summer truce on June 17, awaiting clarification of the new government's policies.

France's former centre-right government was widely accused of holding clandestine negotiations with nationalists, but Chevenement ruled out secret talks. "We have to break with these ambiguous games," he said.

He dodged the question of a possible amnesty for crimes linked to separatism. The leader of A Cuncolta, Francois Santoni, is in preventive detention with about 40 other militants after a crackdown launched last year.
Chevenement, who met police, gendarmes and customs officers, said he was satisfied that the number of arrests this year was double the rate in 1996.
